title: Web Design with JavaScript
blurb: How good websites are designed, then how to build them: buttons, links, pages, sliders, dashboards and dark mode.
intro:
Websites are where most JavaScript lives. This module teaches both halves of making one: design (what the parts of a page are called, where things go, how color and space guide the eye, how dashboards show data) and code (making buttons, links, pages, sliders and forms actually work).

Design stages show a small page and ask you to spot what works and what doesn't. Coding stages have a Page Preview of the Pixel Park game studio site above the editor. Your code runs on that page, and you can click around in it afterwards.

Tip

The DOM & Events section in the Advanced Path covers the building blocks used here (querySelector, classList, addEventListener) in more depth. You can do this module first, and come back to it when something feels new.
links: Nielsen Norman Group: F-shaped reading pattern

stages.hook: Open almost any website and you'll find the same handful of parts in nearly the same places. Designers give each part a name so they can talk about it, and so visitors always know where to look.
stages.l:
Here are the parts nearly every site has, from top to bottom:

PartWhat it holdsWhere it lives
HeaderThe logo (which links home) and the main navigationAcross the very top
Navigation (nav)Links to the main pages. On phones it often folds into a ☰ hamburger buttonInside the header
HeroA big headline, one short sentence, a main button and often a pictureRight under the header
Main contentThe stuff the page is actually about: articles, products, gamesThe middle
SidebarExtras: related links, top scores, filtersBeside the main content
FooterCopyright, contact, privacy and links to every important pageAcross the very bottom

The part of the page you can see before you scroll is called above the fold, a name borrowed from newspapers, where the top half of the front page shows on the stand. Whatever matters most goes above the fold.
stages.p: Look at the Pixel Park page and find the hero.
stages.q: Which letter marks the hero section?
stages.html:
APixel Park
GamesBlogAbout
B

Build your first game this weekend

Free lessons, real projects.

Start free
C

Latest games

Rocket Run
Slime Farm
DTop players
1. Kit
2. Robin
E© Pixel Park · Contact · Privacy
miss: A is the header: the logo and navigation across the top.
C is the main content, the list of games.
E is the footer at the very bottom.
stages.why: B is the hero: the big headline, one line of text and a main button, right under the header. Its job is to tell visitors what the site is and what to do first.
stages.h: Look for the big, bold banner just under the top bar.

stages.p: Visitors don't read websites, they hunt. They expect things in the usual places.
stages.q: Where do visitors expect to find the copyright line, contact details and the privacy policy?
opts: In the header, next to the logo
In the hero, under the headline
In the footer, at the very bottom
In a pop-up when the page opens
miss: The header is prime space for the logo and main links. Legal details would crowd it.
The hero is for your one big message and main button.
Pop-ups that show up uninvited annoy people, and they'll close it without reading.
stages.why: The footer is the site's back cover. People scroll to the bottom on purpose to find contact info, legal links and a full list of pages. Following these habits (designers call it Jakob's Law: people expect your site to work like the other sites they use) makes your site feel easy.
stages.h: Think of the last time you looked for a company's phone number on a website. Where did you scroll to?

stages.l:
A call to action (CTA) is the button that asks the visitor to do the thing the page is for: Start free, Buy now, Play. A page should have one main CTA. It gets the boldest color, sits above the fold, and says exactly what happens when you press it.

Weak CTAStrong CTA
SubmitCreate my account
Click hereDownload the game
Learn more (x5)One bright Start free, plus a quiet See pricing link
Tip

Other buttons can still exist. They just look quieter: an outline instead of a fill, or a plain link.
stages.p: This hero has three buttons that all look exactly the same.
stages.html:
Build your first game this weekend

Free lessons, real projects.

Start free Blog Newsletter
opts: The buttons should be blue, not yellow
Nobody can tell which action matters most
Buttons don't belong in a hero
miss: Yellow on blue stands out well. The color isn't the issue.
More equal buttons makes the choice even harder.
The hero is exactly where the main button belongs.
stages.why: When everything shouts, nothing gets heard. Make Start free the bright main CTA, and turn Blog and Newsletter into quiet outline buttons or links.
stages.h: If you only had two seconds on this page, which button would you press?

stages.l:
HTML has tags named after the parts of a page: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside> (sidebar) and <footer>. They're called landmarks. They look just like a plain <div>, but screen readers let blind visitors jump between them, search engines understand your page better, and your own code becomes easier to read.

JavaScript can find them by tag name, just like by class or id:

const aside = document.querySelector("aside");
const items = aside.querySelectorAll("li");
console.log("Sidebar items: " + items.length);

new Date().getFullYear() gives the current year as a number. Sites use it so the copyright line never goes out of date.
stages.p: Print how many links are in the nav, in the form Nav links: 3. Then put the current year into the footer's #year span using new Date().getFullYear().
stages.h: Search inside the nav with nav.querySelectorAll("a") and use its .length. For the year, set textContent of the span.
stages.html:
Pixel Park
GamesBlogAbout

Welcome!

Lessons and games made by students.

© ???? Pixel Park
stages.reqMsg: Use new Date().getFullYear() so the year updates itself.
stages.st:
// 1. count the links in the nav and print "Nav links: N"

// 2. put this year into #year

stages.l:
People don't read a web page top to bottom. Eye-tracking studies show two common paths:

  • F-pattern on pages full of text: read across the top, then down the left edge, dipping right now and then. Put key words at the start of headings and lines.
  • Z-pattern on simple pages with few words: top-left (logo), across to top-right, diagonally down to bottom-left, then across to bottom-right.
Tip

Both paths start top-left. That's why logos live there, and why dashboards put their most important number there too.
stages.p: This sign-up page has very few words, so eyes travel in a Z.
stages.q: Where should the Join button go so it's the last stop of the Z?
stages.html:
Pixel Park
Log in
Make games with friends
1Bottom-left
2Bottom-right
miss: That's where the eye starts, before it knows what the page is about.
That's the third stop of the Z, not the last.
Position matters a lot. People find buttons in the places they expect.
stages.why: The Z ends bottom-right, after the visitor has read the logo, the top line and the big message. A button there catches them at the moment they're ready to act.
stages.h: Trace a Z with your finger over the page. Where does it end?

stages.l:
Visual hierarchy means the most important thing looks the most important. You control it with:

ToolLouderQuieter
SizeBigSmall
WeightBoldRegular
ColorBright or high contrastGrey or soft
PositionTop, left, centreBottom, edges
SpaceLots of room around itPacked in

A quick test: squint at the page until it's blurry. The first thing you still notice should be the most important thing.
stages.p: Here's a game shop card.
stages.q: What's wrong with this card's hierarchy?
stages.html:
Terms and conditions apply
Rocket Run
$4.99
opts: The least important text is the biggest and boldest
miss: A picture could help, but the bigger problem is what's loud and what's quiet.
The font is fine. Look at the sizes instead.
Squint at it. What do you notice first?
stages.why: The game's name and price should be big and bold, the Buy button clear, and Terms apply small and grey. Size, weight and color tell people what to read first.
stages.h: Squint. Which line jumps out first? Is that what a shopper cares about most?

stages.l:
Our brains treat things that are close together as a group. Designers call this the Law of Proximity (it's one of the Gestalt principles about how we see). Put related things close, and put more space between groups than inside them.

Other ways to group things: a shared background (a card), a line between sections, or the same color for things that do the same job.
stages.p: This form has every label and box spaced exactly the same.
stages.html: <form style="padding:12px;display:grid;gap:14px;max-width:260px"><label>Name</label><input><label>Email</label><input><label>Password</label><input></form>
opts: Put each label right above its box, with bigger gaps between the pairs
miss: Color won't fix which label belongs to which box.
Wider boxes keep the same confusing spacing.
Equal space everywhere is the problem. The space needs to be uneven on purpose.
stages.why: With equal gaps, the label Email sits just as close to the Name box as to its own box. Small gap inside a pair and big gap between pairs makes each label and box read as one unit.
stages.h: Look at the label Email. Is it closer to its own box or to the one above?

stages.l:
Empty space (designers say white space, whatever its color) isn't wasted. It makes pages calm and easy to scan.

To keep spacing consistent, many teams only use multiples of 8 pixels: 8, 16, 24, 32, 48. This is the 8-point grid. Small gaps inside a component (8px), bigger gaps between components (16 to 24px), biggest between sections (32 to 48px). Layouts are also often split into a 12-column grid, since 12 divides into halves, thirds and quarters.

Tip

Buttons and links people tap should be at least about 44px tall on phones. Fingers are much bigger than mouse pointers.
stages.p: A designer is choosing spacing values for a new site.
miss: These are random, so the page will feel slightly off everywhere.
One value for everything means no difference between small and big gaps.
These aren't multiples of 8, and they're too close to each other to tell apart.
stages.why: 8, 16, 24 and 48 are all multiples of 8 and clearly different from each other, so small, medium and large gaps are easy to tell apart.
stages.h: Which set divides evenly by 8?

stages.l:
Lots of sites let you switch how items are laid out: a grid of cards or a list of rows. The trick is that JavaScript doesn't move anything itself. It just adds or removes a class, and the site's CSS already says how each class looks.

const box = document.querySelector(".gallery");
box.classList.add("big");      // CSS for .gallery.big takes over
box.classList.remove("big");   // back to normal
stages.p: Clicking #listBtn should add the class list to .cards. Clicking #gridBtn should remove it. Watch the cards rearrange in the preview.
stages.h: Two click listeners: one calls classList.add("list"), the other classList.remove("list").
stages.html:
Rocket Run
Slime Farm
Pixel Golf
Moon Maze
stages.st: const cards = document.querySelector(".cards");

stages.l:
More than half of all web visits happen on phones. A site that adjusts to any screen size is called responsive. Common moves when the screen gets narrow:

  • Side-by-side columns stack into one column.
  • The nav folds into a ☰ hamburger menu.
  • Text stays at least 16px, and buttons get bigger, not smaller.

Many designers sketch the phone version first, then add columns as the screen grows. It forces you to decide what really matters.
stages.p: A page has three columns of cards side by side on a laptop. Now it's on a phone 375 pixels wide.
stages.q: What do most well-designed sites do?
opts: Shrink all three columns until the text is tiny
Stack the cards into one column
miss: Tiny text is unreadable on a phone.
Hiding content means phone visitors miss things.
Sideways scrolling is awkward and easy to miss.
stages.why: Stacking keeps every card readable at full size. Visitors on phones are used to scrolling down, not sideways.
stages.h: Think of your favorite site on your phone. Do things sit side by side, or one under another?

stages.l:
Colors carry meaning before anyone reads a word. On the web, people have learned a few strong habits:

ColorUsually means
GreenSuccess, done, go, money
RedError, danger, delete, stop
YellowWarning, careful, attention
BlueLinks, trust, calm (banks and social sites love it)
GreyDisabled, less important, background details

Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) feel energetic and jump forward. Cool colors (blue, green, purple) feel calm and sit back. That's why a warm button pops on a cool page.

Watch out

About 1 in 12 boys can't tell some reds and greens apart. Never use color alone: add an icon or a word too, like ✓ Saved or ✗ Error.
stages.p: A shop shows this message after someone pays.
stages.html: Your payment worked! Thanks for your order.
opts: Red says something went wrong, but the news is good
miss: Short is good for a status message.
A pop-up wouldn't fix the mixed signal.
Corners won't confuse anyone. The color will.
stages.why: People see red and think error before they read a word. Success messages should be green, with a ✓ so color isn't the only clue.
stages.h: If you only saw the color, without reading, what would you think happened?

stages.l:
A simple recipe for a palette that feels balanced:

  • 60% a calm main color, usually a light or dark neutral for the background.
  • 30% a secondary color for big areas like the header, cards and sidebar.
  • 10% an accent color, saved for the things you want clicked: the main button, links, highlights.

Pixel Park uses light grey for 60%, navy for 30% and gold for 10%. Look back at the earlier pages: gold only shows up on the main button.

Tip

The accent only works because it's rare. If every button is gold, none of them stands out.
stages.p: Four students describe their site's colors.
opts: Everything bright orange so it feels exciting
White background, dark green header and cards, pink only on the Buy buttons
Equal amounts of red, blue and yellow
A different color for every section
miss: With orange everywhere, nothing can stand out.
Equal amounts means no main color and no accent.
Too many colors makes a page feel messy and hard to scan.
stages.why: White is the calm 60%, dark green is the 30% for big areas, and pink is the rare 10% accent that pulls eyes to the Buy buttons.
stages.h: Look for one big calm color, one supporting color, and one rare bright one.

stages.l:
Contrast is the difference in brightness between text and its background. The web's accessibility rules (WCAG) give it a number from 1:1 (no difference) to 21:1 (black on white):

TextNeeds at least
Normal text4.5 : 1
Large text (24px, or bold 19px)3 : 1
Icons and button borders3 : 1

Low contrast is one of the most common problems on the web. Light grey on white looks stylish on a bright monitor and disappears on a phone in sunlight.
stages.p: Here are four button styles.
stages.q: Which one is easiest for everyone to read?
opts: Start free Gold text on white
Start free Grey text on white
Start free White text on navy
Start free Red text on green
miss: Gold on white is only about 1.8 : 1. Many people can barely see it.
Light grey on white is about 2.9 : 1, below the 4.5 : 1 rule.
Red on green is low contrast and invisible to many color-blind people.
stages.why: White on navy is about 14 : 1, way past the 4.5 : 1 minimum. Strong contrast helps everyone: people with low vision, tired eyes, old screens or bright sunlight.
stages.h: Which pair is most different in brightness, not just in color?

stages.hook: A designer hands you the color #ff8800. To check its contrast, your code needs to know how much red, green and blue are inside. How do you get numbers out of that string?
stages.l: A hex color is three pairs of base-16 digits: red, green, blue. Each pair runs from 00 (none) to ff (full).
stages.p: What does this program print?
miss: slice(1, 3) takes characters 1 and 2 only.
slice starts at index 1, which skips the #.
parseInt with 16 reads ff as a base-16 number, and ff is the biggest two-digit hex value.
stages.why: slice(1, 3) takes the characters at index 1 and 2, which is ff. parseInt(text, 16) reads text as a base-16 number: f is 15, so ff is 15 × 16 + 15 = 255, full red.
stages.h: Count positions from 0: # is 0, f is 1, f is 2. Then remember ff in hex is the biggest two-digit value.

stages.l:
Each pair of a hex color sits at a fixed spot: red at index 1 to 3, green at 3 to 5, blue at 5 to 7. Slice each one out and turn it into a number with parseInt(pair, 16).

const hex = "#00ccff";
const blue = parseInt(hex.slice(5, 7), 16);
console.log(blue); // 255
255
stages.p: Write hexToRgb(hex) that returns an array [red, green, blue] of numbers. hexToRgb("#ff8800") should return [255, 136, 0].
stages.h: Use the same slice-and-parse as the example three times, with the start index 1, 3 and 5, and return all three in an array.

stages.l:
Real design tools check contrast with a formula from the WCAG rules. The starter already has luminance(hex), which says how bright a color looks (0 is black, 1 is white). The contrast ratio is:

(brighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05)

The brighter one always goes on top, whichever color you pass first. Math.max and Math.min sort that out.

const big = Math.max(0.2, 0.9);   // 0.9
const small = Math.min(0.2, 0.9); // 0.2
console.log(Math.round(3.14159 * 100) / 100); // 3.14
stages.p: Write contrast(a, b) that returns the contrast ratio of two hex colors, rounded to 2 decimal places. Black and white should give 21, white and white 1, and #777777 on white 4.48 (just under the 4.5 rule!).
stages.h: Get both luminances first. Then use Math.max for the brighter and Math.min for the darker, plug them into the formula, and round with Math.round(x * 100) / 100.

stages.l:
Big sites don't write the same color in fifty places. They store it once in a CSS variable (its name starts with --) and every rule uses var(--name). Change the variable and the whole site changes at once.

/* in the site's CSS */
.btn { background: var(--brand); }

JavaScript can change a variable with style.setProperty:

document.body.style.setProperty("--size", "20px");

In these previews, document.body is the whole preview page. Each swatch button also stores its color in a data-color attribute, which you can read with button.dataset.color.
stages.p: When any .swatch button is clicked, set the --accent variable on document.body to that button's data-color. Try the swatches in the preview and watch the button and links change.
stages.h: Loop over document.querySelectorAll(".swatch") and give each one a click listener that calls document.body.style.setProperty("--accent", btn.dataset.color).
stages.html:
Pixel Park
GamesBlog

Pick an accent color:

Start free See all games ›
stages.reqMsg: Change the CSS variable with style.setProperty("--accent", ...).
stages.st: const swatches = document.querySelectorAll(".swatch");

stages.l:
Dark mode is just a class. The site's CSS has a second set of colors for .dark, and the switch toggles that class on and off.

panel.classList.toggle("open"); // adds it if missing, removes it if there
const isOpen = panel.classList.contains("open");

A switch should also say what it does next, and tell screen readers whether it's on with aria-pressed.
stages.p: Clicking #theme toggles the class dark on document.body. When dark mode is on, the button reads ☀ Light mode and has aria-pressed="true". When it's off, it reads ☾ Dark mode with aria-pressed="false".
stages.h: Inside the click listener: toggle the class, then check classList.contains("dark") and set the button's textContent and setAttribute("aria-pressed", ...) to match.
stages.html:
Pixel Park

Latest games

Rocket Run
Slime Farm
stages.st: const btn = document.querySelector("#theme");

stages.l:
A dashboard shows the important numbers about something on one screen: a game's players, a shop's sales, a school's grades. A good one answers its main question at a glance, in about five seconds.

Most dashboards use three bands, from most to least important:

  1. KPI tiles across the top. A KPI (key performance indicator) is one big number that matters, like Players today. Keep it to about 3 to 6.
  2. Charts in the middle, showing trends and comparisons.
  3. Detail tables at the bottom, for people who want to dig in.
Tip

Eyes start top-left, so that's where the single most important number goes, biggest of all.
stages.p: Here's a dashboard for the Pixel Park game servers.
stages.q: Which letter marks the KPI tiles?
stages.html:
APlayers today
1,284
New sign-ups
96
Games played
5,310

3
BPlayers per day
CRecent players
Kit · 32 min · Rocket Run
Robin · 14 min · Slime Farm
miss: B is a chart showing a trend over time.
C is a detail table with individual players.
stages.why: A is the row of KPI tiles: a few big numbers across the top, with the most important one, Players today, in the top-left and the largest.
stages.h: KPIs are single big numbers.

stages.l:
Each kind of chart answers a different kind of question:

QuestionBest choice
How did it change over time?Line chart
Which category is biggest?Bar chart (sorted biggest first)
What's the one number right now?KPI tile with an arrow showing up or down
How close are we to a goal?Progress bar
What are the exact details?Table
Watch out

Pie charts with lots of slices are hard to read, because people are bad at comparing angles. A sorted bar chart is almost always clearer.
stages.p: The Pixel Park team wants to see how many people visited the site each day over the last 30 days.
miss: 30 slices would be impossible to compare.
One number can't show how it changed across the month.
A table has the numbers, but you can't see the trend at a glance.
stages.why: Change over time is exactly what line charts are for. The eye follows the line and instantly sees whether it's going up or down.
stages.h: The question is about change over time.

stages.l:
Real dashboards don't have numbers typed into the HTML. The numbers arrive as data (usually an array of objects) and JavaScript builds the tiles.

const tags = ["new", "hot"];
const box = document.querySelector(".tags");
for (const t of tags) {
  const span = document.createElement("span");
  span.className = "pill";
  span.textContent = t;
  box.append(span);
}
stages.p: For each item in stats, add a div with class kpi to #kpis. Inside it, put a <b> holding the value and a <span> holding the label. Tip: innerHTML with a template string is fine here, because you wrote the data yourself.
stages.h: Loop with for (const s of stats), create the div, give it className = "kpi", fill it with `<b>${s.value}</b><span>${s.label}</span>` and append it to #kpis.
stages.html: Today

stages.l:
1284 is harder to read than 1,284, and 4999.5 is worse than $4,999.50. toLocaleString formats numbers the way people expect in their country:

const n = 2500000;
console.log(n.toLocaleString("en-US"));            // 2,500,000
console.log((0.25).toLocaleString("en-US", { style: "percent" }));  // 25%
console.log((9.5).toLocaleString("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" })); // €9.50
stages.p: Show players in #players as 12,345, sales in #sales as US dollars ($4,999.50), and growth in #growth as a percent (8%).
stages.h: Use toLocaleString("en-US") for players, add { style: "currency", currency: "USD" } for sales and { style: "percent" } for growth. Put each result in the element's textContent.
stages.html:
Players

Sales

Growth
stages.reqMsg: Format the numbers with toLocaleString instead of typing the text yourself.

stages.l:
A progress bar is two boxes: a grey track and a colored fill inside it. JavaScript sets the fill's width as a percent.

const pct = Math.round(30 / 120 * 100);   // 25
fill.style.width = pct + "%";

Careful: if someone beats the goal, the percent goes over 100 and the bar pokes out of its track. Math.min(pct, 100) caps it.
stages.p: For each goal in goals, find the bar with the matching data-goal attribute (like .bar[data-goal="lessons"]). Set its .fill width to the percent done, capped at 100, and put the percent text (like 25%) in its .pct. Show the real percent there even when it's over 100.
stages.h: Loop over the goals. Build the selector with a template string: `.bar[data-goal="${g.id}"]`. Work out the percent with Math.round, then set style.width with Math.min.
stages.html:
Weekly goals

Lessons
Games built
Minutes coded

stages.l:
You don't need a chart library for a simple bar chart. Each bar is a div whose height is a percent of the tallest value, so the biggest bar fills the chart.

const scores = [4, 10, 7];
const top = Math.max(...scores);       // 10
console.log(scores.map(s => s / top * 100)); // [40, 100, 70]
[ 40, 100, 70 ]
stages.p: For each game in plays, add a div with class col to #chart. Set its style.height to its share of the biggest value as a percent (the biggest is 100%), and its title to the game name. Inside it, put the game name as text.
stages.h: Find the biggest with Math.max(...plays.map(p => p.count)). Then loop, create each div, and set style.height = (p.count / top * 100) + "%".
stages.html: Plays this week

stages.t: Up or down at a glance
stages.l:
A number alone doesn't say if things are good. Dashboards add a trend: green and ▲ for up, red and ▼ for down. Remember the rule from earlier: never color alone, so the arrow matters as much as the color.

const temp = -3;
const label = temp < 0 ? "freezing" : "fine";
el.classList.add(temp < 0 ? "cold" : "warm");
stages.p: Each .trend has a data-change number. If it's above 0, add class up and set its text to ▲ plus the number (like ▲ 12). If it's below 0, add class down and use ▼ plus the number without its minus sign (▼ 4). If it's exactly 0, add class flat and show – 0.
stages.h: Turn el.dataset.change into a number with Number(). Use Math.abs(n) to drop the minus sign. An if / else if / else handles the three cases.

stages.l:
Dashboards and shops let you narrow down a list: All, Open, Done. Each item carries a data- attribute, and the filter hides items that don't match by setting their hidden property.

for (const row of rows) {
  row.hidden = row.dataset.size !== "big";
}
stages.p: Each .filter button has a data-show of all, open or done. Clicking one hides every li whose data-status doesn't match (all shows everything) and gives that button the class active, removing it from the others.
stages.h: In each button's click listener, read btn.dataset.show. Loop the lis and set li.hidden = show !== "all" && li.dataset.status !== show. Then loop the buttons and use classList.toggle("active", b === btn).
stages.html:
Bug tracker

  • Player falls through floor
  • Score resets on pause
  • Music too loud
  • Typo on title screen
stages.st:
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll(".filter");
const items = document.querySelectorAll("#bugs li");

stages.hook: Everything up to now was about how a site looks. Now it needs to do things. Every like, add-to-cart and play button on the web works the same way: wait for a click, then change something on the page.
stages.l:
Use a real <button> for anything that does something, and a link (<a>) for anything that goes somewhere. Buttons work with the keyboard and screen readers for free.

let stars = 0;
const starBtn = document.querySelector("#star");
starBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
  stars++;
  starBtn.textContent = "★ " + stars;
});
Tip

Good buttons give feedback straight away: the count changes, the color changes, or the label changes. If nothing visible happens, people click again and again.
stages.p: Make the #like button work. Each click adds 1 to likes, shows the new number in #count, and adds the class liked to the button (so it turns pink).
stages.h: Same shape as the star example: a click listener that adds 1 to likes, then updates #count's textContent and calls classList.add("liked") on the button.
stages.html:
Rocket Run

Dodge asteroids, grab fuel, reach the moon.

0 likes

stages.l: A button that only works once should say so: change its label and disable it, so nobody subscribes twice.

stages.h: Find both elements first. Then the listener opens, does its three jobs, and closes.

stages.l:
A link needs an href (where it goes) and text (what people click). Links to other sites usually open in a new tab with target="_blank", plus rel="noopener" so the other site can't reach back and mess with yours.

const docs = document.querySelector("#docs");
docs.setAttribute("href", "https://developer.mozilla.org");
docs.setAttribute("target", "_blank");   // open in a new tab
docs.setAttribute("rel", "noopener");    // keep our page safe

You can also set them as properties, like link.href = ..., which is shorter.

Tip

Link text should make sense on its own. Screen reader users often jump from link to link, so ten links that all say click here are useless.
stages.p: Build the nav from links. For each one, add an a to the nav with its href and text. If external is true, also set target to _blank and rel to noopener.
stages.h: Loop over links, create an a, set href and textContent, and use an if (link.external) for the extra two properties. Append each one to the nav.

stages.l:
A website can have many pages in two ways. A multi-page site has a separate HTML file for each page, and every link loads a whole new page. A single-page app (SPA) loads once and JavaScript swaps which section is showing. Games, Gmail and most dashboards work like this, because switching is instant.

The simplest SPA: every page is a section with a data-page name, and only one is visible at a time. The nav links say which page they want with data-link.

function showTab(name) {
  document.querySelectorAll(".tab").forEach(t => {
    t.hidden = t.dataset.tab !== name;
  });
}

Two more details make it feel right. event.preventDefault() stops the browser following the link the normal way, and aria-current="page" marks the link for the page you're on (the site's CSS underlines it in gold).
stages.p: Clicking a nav link shows only the .view whose data-page matches the link's data-link, and hides the others. The clicked link gets aria-current="page", and the other links lose it (use removeAttribute).
stages.h: Give each nav a a click listener. Inside it: e.preventDefault(), read link.dataset.link, loop over the .views setting hidden, then loop over the links calling setAttribute or removeAttribute.

Every site needs a plan for addresses that don't exist: a 404 page (404 is the web's error code for "not found"). A good one is friendly and links back home.

A clean way to organise a single-page site is one function, often called a router, that takes a page name and shows it. Then links, buttons and the start-up code all call the same function.

const sizes = ["small", "medium", "large"];

stages.l:
Long one-page sites jump to a section when you click its nav link. The page scrolls so the section's top lines up with the top of the window.

const box = document.querySelector("#faq");
console.log(box.offsetTop);   // how far down the page it starts
window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "smooth" }); // glide back to the top

offsetTop is how many pixels from the top of the page an element starts. window.scrollTo scrolls there, and behavior: "smooth" makes it glide instead of jump, so people can tell where they went.
stages.p: Each nav link has a data-to with the id of its section. When a link is clicked, stop the normal link behavior and smoothly scroll the window to that section's offsetTop.
stages.h: Find the section with document.getElementById(link.dataset.to), then window.scrollTo({ top: section.offsetTop, behavior: "smooth" }).

On long pages, a small back to top button saves a lot of scrolling. It should only appear once you've scrolled down, or it just gets in the way.

The window fires a scroll event every time the page moves, and window.scrollY says how far down it is.

window.addEventListener("scroll", () => {

stages.l:
Blogs often show a thin bar at the top that fills up as you read. To work out the percent, you need how far you've scrolled and how far you can scroll:

const page = document.body;
const most = page.scrollHeight - page.clientHeight; // the furthest you can scroll
console.log(most);

scrollHeight is the full height of the content, and clientHeight is the part you can see.
stages.p: Every time the page scrolls, set the width of #bar to how far down the reader is, as a percent (0% at the top, 100% at the bottom).
stages.h: In a scroll listener, divide window.scrollY by document.body.scrollHeight - document.body.clientHeight, multiply by 100, and set bar.style.width to that plus "%".

stages.l:
A slider (or carousel) shows one slide at a time with ‹ and › buttons. The whole thing runs on one number: the index of the current slide. The % (remainder) operator makes it wrap around, so › on the last slide goes back to the first.

const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
let i = 2;
i = (i + 1) % colors.length;                  // 0, wrapped to the start
i = (i - 1 + colors.length) % colors.length;  // 2, wrapped to the end
stages.p: Write show() so only slides[index] is visible and #where reads like 2 / 4. #next moves forward and #prev moves back, both wrapping around. Call show() once at the start.
stages.h: In show(), loop with forEach((s, n) => s.hidden = n !== index) and set #where to (index + 1) + " / " + slides.length. Each button changes index with % as in the example, then calls show().

An <input type="range"> is a slider you drag. It fires an input event every time it moves, and its value is always a string, so turn it into a number when you need to do math.

volume.addEventListener("input", () => {

Tip

Always show the current value next to a slider. Otherwise people have to guess what setting they chose.

The button should tell screen readers whether the menu is open with aria-expanded, which is "true" or "false" as a string.

const open = drawer.classList.toggle("show"); // toggle returns true if it's now on

stages.l:
A modal is a box that pops up over the page and needs an answer before you carry on: a sign-in form, "Are you sure?", a big picture. Every modal needs a clear way out: a ✕ button, and the Escape key.

document.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
  if (e.key === "Enter") console.log("Enter pressed");
});
Watch out

Don't open pop-ups the moment a page loads. People haven't even seen your site yet, and most will close it without reading.
stages.p: #openBtn shows #modal (set hidden to false). #closeBtn hides it, and so does pressing the Escape key.
stages.h: Three listeners. The keydown one checks e.key === "Escape" before hiding the modal.

stages.l:
Forms are how websites listen: sign-ups, searches, messages. Before sending anything, check the answers and explain problems in words, next to the form, not just with a red border.

form.addEventListener("submit", e => {
  e.preventDefault();          // stay on this page
  const name = nameBox.value.trim();
  if (name === "") error.textContent = "Please add your name.";
});

.trim() removes spaces from both ends, so a box with only spaces counts as empty.
stages.p: When the form is submitted: if the email doesn't include @, put Please enter a valid email. in #err. Otherwise, if the message (trimmed) is shorter than 10 characters, put Please write at least 10 characters. in #err. If both are fine, clear #err, hide the form and show #thanks.
stages.h: In the submit listener: e.preventDefault(), read both .values, then an if / else if / else. Use email.includes("@") and message.trim().length < 10.
